correctness.rationale: For a connected subset \(C\) of the orbit space, the first coordinate is fixed. If the \(n\)-th projection is the singleton \(\{a_n\}\), then the next projection is a connected subset of the totally disconnected fiber \(F(a_n)\), hence again a singleton. Induction makes every coordinate constant, so \(C\) is a point. Nondegeneracy independently removes isolated orbits: in any basic product neighborhood, keep a sufficiently long prefix, choose a different allowed next point in the nondegenerate fiber, and extend recursively. Upper semicontinuity with compact values gives a closed graph and hence a closed orbit set in compact metrizable \(X^{\mathbb N}\). Thus the nonempty orbit set is compact, metrizable, perfect and totally disconnected, which characterizes the Cantor set. This also pinpoints why finiteness in the source's Theorem 3.16 is unnecessary.

value.rationale: The theorem answers an explicit open question by isolating the separate roles of compactness, total disconnectedness and nondegeneracy. The proof removes the finite-fiber restriction in a natural orbit-space theorem and gives a clean structural criterion useful in set-valued dynamics.

final_claim: Let \(X\) be compact metric and \(F:X\to2^X\) upper semicontinuous with nonempty compact values. If every fiber \(F(x)\) is nondegenerate and totally disconnected, then every fixed-base forward orbit set \(\mathcal O_F(z)\) is homeomorphic to the Cantor set.
limitations: The conclusion is qualitative; it gives no metric dimension or dynamical-complexity estimate.
Upper semicontinuity is used for closedness/compactness of the orbit set; the internal total-disconnectedness and no-isolated-points arguments use weaker hypotheses.
